words.etymology: Named from the French envoy (messenger or representative) — Envoy acts as an intermediary on behalf of each service, handling all communications so the service itself can focus on its business logic. Created by Matt Klein at Lyft and open-sourced in September 2016.

words.shortDefinition: The query-optimized data store maintained separately from the write model in a CQRS architecture.
words.simpleDefinition: In CQRS, the read model is the query side's data store — shaped specifically for the queries that clients will execute. It is denormalized, pre-joined, and stored in whatever technology answers queries fastest for its access patterns: a flat document store, a search index, a key-value cache, or a materialized view. It is derived from the write model via projections and is never written to directly by client commands.
words.longDefinition: The read model is the distinguishing half of CQRS's split. In the CQRS chapter of Microservices Patterns, the read model has two defining characteristics: it is derived (never receives direct writes from clients — all data flows through the write model and then through projections), and it is eventually consistent (it reflects the write model as of some recent point in time, with a delay bounded by projection throughput). A service may maintain multiple read models simultaneously, each shaped for a different consumer's query pattern. The order management example from the book illustrates this: one MongoDB document store serves the customer portal (flat document per order, indexed by customerId), one Redis sorted set serves the warehouse fulfillment queue (orders scored by urgency per warehouse), and one columnar store feeds the analytics dashboard. Each projection is independent — a failure in the analytics projection does not affect the customer portal. The read model can use a completely different storage technology from the write model, chosen for the specific access patterns it serves: a relational DB for the write model (normalized, transactional), Elasticsearch for a search read model, Redis for a cache read model. Because the read model is disposable and derived, it can be rebuilt at any time by replaying events. This makes schema evolution on the read side far safer than on a unified model: if the read model schema needs to change, add a new projection and rebuild the read store from events — no risky data migration required.
words.connector: Think of the read model like a pre-printed report generated from raw data. The raw data (write model) is the authoritative source; the report (read model) is derived from it in a format optimized for quick reading. You can generate as many different report formats as you need — all from the same raw data.
words.techContext: Our customer-portal read model is a MongoDB collection with one document per order, pre-joining customer name and address, so the portal API requires zero cross-service calls and answers in under 5ms.
words.exampleSentence: We rebuilt the read model for the fulfillment dashboard by adding a new Kafka consumer projection without touching the write model — the new view was populated from historical events within an hour.
words.etymology: Read model is CQRS-specific terminology introduced by Greg Young and Udi Dahan around 2009-2010. The term explicitly labels the query-side data representation to contrast it with the write model — the two halves of the CQRS split.

words.shortDefinition: The authoritative command-handling side of CQRS that enforces business rules and persists state.
words.simpleDefinition: In CQRS, the write model is the command side's data store — the authoritative source of truth. It validates commands, enforces all business invariants, records state changes transactionally, and publishes events or change notifications that projections use to update the read model. It is normalized for correctness, not optimized for queries — clients never query it directly.
words.longDefinition: The write model is the command side of the CQRS split. In the CQRS chapter of Microservices Patterns, its responsibilities are: validation (reject commands that violate business rules — an order cannot be placed if the customer's account is suspended), invariant enforcement (ensure aggregate consistency — no line item added after order is confirmed), persistence (write authoritative state atomically, with full transactional integrity as the single source of truth), and change publication (emit an event or notification via the Outbox pattern so projections can update the read model asynchronously). The write model is not optimized for queries. Its schema is normalized for correctness: in an order management system, orders and line items are stored in separate normalized tables with full referential integrity. This normalization may require multi-table joins for complex queries — but those joins are the read model's problem, not the write model's. Because the write model is not queried directly by clients, it can evolve its internal schema without breaking query APIs. Its only external contract is the events it emits. In DDD terms, the write model aligns naturally with aggregates: each command targets one aggregate root, the aggregate enforces invariants, and the transaction boundary matches the aggregate boundary. When combined with event sourcing, the write model stores the event log rather than mutable state — the aggregate replays events to rehydrate rather than reading a current-state row.
words.connector: Think of the write model like the official registry of a city — it records deeds, births, and marriages with full legal validity and strict procedural requirements. Citizens don't query the official registry for every lookup (too slow, wrong format) — they use derived directories and databases. But the registry is the source of truth that all derived data must ultimately match.
words.techContext: Our write model is a normalized PostgreSQL schema using the Outbox pattern — every order state change writes to the orders table and an outbox table in one transaction, guaranteeing event publication without dual-write risk.
words.exampleSentence: The write model rejects the AddItem command if the order is already confirmed — this invariant is enforced once, in the aggregate root, and cannot be bypassed by querying around it.
words.etymology: Write model is CQRS-specific terminology introduced alongside read model by Greg Young and Udi Dahan around 2009-2010. The symmetry of the names (write model / read model) makes the CQRS split explicit in code and conversation.

words.shortDefinition: Rebuilding the state of an entity as it existed at a specific point in time by replaying events up to that moment.
words.simpleDefinition: A temporal query answers the question: what did this entity look like at time T? In a CRUD system, yesterday's state is gone unless an audit table was built separately. In an event-sourced system, every historical state is recoverable by replaying the event stream up to a specific version number or timestamp. This capability is a natural consequence of the immutable event log — history is not overwritten, it accumulates.
words.longDefinition: Temporal queries are covered in the event sourcing chapter of Microservices Patterns as a first-class benefit of the append-only event log. Because events are stored with sequence numbers and timestamps and are never deleted or modified, the state of any aggregate at any past point can be reconstructed by filtering and replaying the relevant subset of events. Two forms of temporal query: by event version (replay events 0 through version N to recover state at version N — deterministic and independent of wall-clock time, useful for debugging specific state transitions) and by timestamp (filter events with recorded timestamp before or equal to target time T, then replay — requires accurate timestamps and care around clock skew). Temporal queries are valuable in several production scenarios: debugging production incidents (what was the order's exact state when the payment service made its decision?); regulatory compliance (what was the customer's account balance on a specific regulatory reporting date?); reproducing production bugs in test environments (seed the test with real production events up to the moment of failure); auditing (who changed what and when, across the full history of an entity). The critical prerequisite for reliable temporal queries is that the event log is genuinely the single source of truth — if any state changes were made outside the event sourcing path (direct database updates, batch imports), those changes are invisible to temporal queries and the reconstructed state will be wrong.
words.connector: Think of a temporal query like rewinding a documentary to a specific timestamp and pausing it. Because the entire film was recorded and preserved, you can see exactly what the scene looked like at any moment — something impossible if the film were edited in place as events occurred.
words.techContext: During a disputed insurance claim, we used a temporal query to reconstruct the exact policy state on the date of the alleged incident — answering a question that would have been impossible without event sourcing.
words.exampleSentence: The auditor's request to see every customer's subscription status as of the quarter-end date took 20 minutes to implement as a temporal query, compared to the three days it would have required without event sourcing.
words.etymology: Temporal (from Latin temporalis, of or relating to time) + query (a request for information). The term is established in database theory (temporal databases, bitemporal modeling) and was adopted into event sourcing to describe the time-travel capability the append-only log enables.

words.shortDefinition: Deliberately running tests or experiments against live production traffic (canaries, dark launches, chaos).
words.simpleDefinition: Testing in production is the intentional practice of validating software behavior using real production traffic, users, and infrastructure — not only in isolated staging environments. Techniques include canary deployments (expose a fraction of real users to a new version), dark launches (run new code against mirrored real traffic without exposing results), chaos engineering (inject failures into production to test resilience), and A/B experiments (compare behavioral metrics between two user groups in production).
words.longDefinition: The Microservices Patterns book's testing chapter includes testing in production as a frontier technique that acknowledges a fundamental limitation of pre-production testing: staging environments cannot fully replicate the scale, data diversity, traffic patterns, and interaction complexity of real production. Key techniques under the testing-in-production umbrella: canary deployments expose a controlled percentage of real users to a new version while observing real metrics; dark launches mirror production traffic to a new version and compare outputs without affecting users; chaos engineering deliberately injects failures (latency, errors, pod terminations) to validate resilience properties under real load; feature flag experiments route users to different behaviors and measure real business metrics rather than synthetic benchmarks; load testing in production (with appropriate circuit breakers and kill switches) validates performance at real scale. The practice requires strong observability: without metrics, logs, and traces showing what the production system is doing, testing in production provides signals with no interpretation. It also requires safety mechanisms: automatic rollback triggers, kill switches, traffic percentage caps, and blast-radius limits. Organizations that practice testing in production most effectively (Netflix, LinkedIn, Amazon, Google) combine it with strong pre-production testing — testing in production complements the testing pyramid, it does not replace the lower layers. The ethical dimension: testing that can affect real users or real transactions requires clear accountability, rollback plans, and appropriate disclosure in regulated industries.
words.connector: Think of testing in production like a race car manufacturer using real race conditions to validate performance — not just treadmills and wind tunnels. The controlled chaos of real race conditions reveals failure modes that no simulated test environment could replicate. The car is instrumented to record everything, and the team has safety systems ready to intervene if something fails dangerously.
words.techContext: Our chaos engineering practice runs weekly scheduled GameDays in production, terminating random pod instances during low-traffic periods to verify our services recover without manual intervention.
words.exampleSentence: Testing in production via traffic mirroring validated the new recommendation engine against actual user behavior for two weeks before any real user experienced its output.
words.etymology: The phrase was coined and popularized by Charity Majors (Honeycomb) and others in the observability community around 2017-2018, challenging the assumption that production environments should be exclusively for verified, complete software.

words.shortDefinition: Partitioning a system into independently deployable, self-contained cells that share no infrastructure, limiting the blast radius of failures.
words.simpleDefinition: Cell-based architecture divides a large distributed system into multiple isolated, independently deployable cells — each a complete, self-contained copy of the service stack serving a subset of traffic (a tenant range, a geographic region, or a hash-assigned user group). Cells share no runtime infrastructure: not databases, not caches, not message brokers. A failure in one cell is bounded to that cell's traffic subset, while all other cells continue unaffected.
words.longDefinition: Cell-based architecture is the structural evolution of fault isolation from the service level to the full-stack level. While fault isolation (bulkheads, circuit breakers) limits failure propagation within a service, cell-based architecture prevents failure propagation across the entire fleet by ensuring that cells have zero shared mutable runtime state. The design is most applicable to large multi-tenant SaaS platforms and to systems with very high availability requirements where even a well-isolated service-level failure affecting all tenants is unacceptable. Architecture: a router or API gateway at the edge maps incoming traffic to a cell — by tenant ID, user ID hash, or geographic region. Each cell contains a complete set of services, its own databases, its own message broker topics, and its own cache clusters. A failure in cell 3 (a database crash, a bad deployment, an infrastructure incident) affects only cell 3's tenants; cells 1, 2, and 4 are entirely unaffected. Cell-based architecture is used by Slack (shards for workspace isolation), AWS (availability zones are physical cells; AZ-aware deployments are logical cells), and large e-commerce platforms (tenant-based cell routing). Trade-offs: significant infrastructure cost (N cells × full stack), cross-cell operations require explicit coordination (a cross-tenant query must fan out to all cells), cell sizing requires capacity modeling, and tenant redistribution (moving a tenant from one cell to another) requires data migration tooling. Cell-based architecture is most justified at the scale where a single-stack deployment's blast radius is too large for the business to accept — where any production incident affecting all customers costs more than the additional infrastructure overhead of cell isolation.
words.connector: Think of cell-based architecture like a hospital divided into independent wards, each with its own staff, supplies, and power circuit. If a plumbing failure floods one ward, the other wards continue operating normally. The redundancy is expensive, but no single failure can take the entire hospital offline.
words.techContext: We implemented a three-cell architecture for our enterprise SaaS platform, assigning tenants to cells by hash — a database incident in cell 2 affected only 33% of tenants rather than the entire fleet.
words.exampleSentence: Cell-based architecture bounded the blast radius of a botched database migration to one cell's 800 tenants while the remaining 2400 tenants across the other cells experienced no disruption.
words.etymology: Cell from Latin cella ('small room, compartment') — used in biology for the basic unit of life (each self-contained), and in computing by analogy to describe a self-contained unit of infrastructure. Cell-based architecture was documented and popularized by AWS, Slack, and large-scale SaaS operators as a formal pattern for blast-radius reduction.

words.shortDefinition: The immutable, ordered sequence of events that is the source of truth in event sourcing.
words.simpleDefinition: The append-only event log is the foundational data structure of event sourcing: an ordered sequence of immutable facts where new events are always written to the end and nothing is ever updated or deleted. It is the single source of truth from which any past or present state can be derived. Its permanence and immutability are not limitations — they are the design: history is the data, and the data is the history.
words.longDefinition: The Microservices Patterns book's event sourcing chapter describes the append-only event log as the most consequential design choice in event sourcing, with three defining properties that distinguish it from ordinary database tables and message queues: append-only (the only write operation is appending to the end — no UPDATE, no DELETE, no PATCH; a mistake is corrected by a new correction event, not an edit to the original); immutable (once written, an event cannot be changed; this is not just a technical constraint but a semantic claim — an event says this occurred, and that occurrence cannot be undone, only acknowledged and corrected); ordered (events carry sequence numbers establishing causal order within a stream, and replay depends on this ordering being stable). In practice the log is partitioned by aggregate stream: one stream per aggregate instance (Order-4821, Order-4822), each with its own sequence number starting at zero. EventStoreDB (Kurrent) calls these streams; Marten calls them aggregate streams. Optimistic concurrency control is implemented by asserting the expected stream version on write — if two concurrent writers both try to append at version 7, one succeeds and the other receives a concurrency conflict. This replaces row-level locking with a compare-and-swap at the log level. Storage concerns: event logs grow indefinitely — unlike CRUD databases where updates and deletes manage storage, event stores only grow. Data retention policies, archival strategies, and compliance frameworks (GDPR right-to-erasure via cryptographic erasure) require planning from the start. The append-only log also enables Kafka-style event streaming when combined with a broker: events appended to the log can be published to Kafka topics, making the event store both the system of record and the event stream source.
words.connector: Think of the append-only event log like the flight data recorder (black box) on an aircraft. It continuously records every sensor reading and control input; nothing is ever erased. After a flight, any moment in the journey can be reconstructed precisely from the recording — the recording is both the operational log and the investigation tool.
words.techContext: Our EventStoreDB event log for the trading system has grown to 800 million events over 5 years — each trade, modification, and cancellation permanently recorded and available for both real-time processing and historical audit queries.
words.exampleSentence: The append-only event log meant that when a bug in the pricing engine produced incorrect order totals for 3 hours, we could replay the affected orders through the corrected engine and produce accurate reconciliation records without any manual data correction.
words.etymology: Append-only (adding to the end, never modifying) + event (something that occurred) + log (an ordered record of events). The combination describes the Kafka log concept generalized to domain events, with immutability as a first-class property. The pattern connects to Pat Helland's 2007 paper 'Life beyond Distributed Transactions' and to the database WAL (Write-Ahead Log) which is also append-only.

words.shortDefinition: Building an internal developer platform — self-service tooling, standardized pipelines, and golden paths — so product teams ship faster with less cognitive overhead.
words.simpleDefinition: Platform engineering is the discipline of building and operating an internal developer platform (IDP) that abstracts away infrastructure complexity so product teams can provision services, deploy code, and manage observability through self-service interfaces. Instead of every team independently managing Kubernetes configuration, CI/CD pipelines, secrets, and monitoring, the platform team builds and maintains these capabilities as a product for internal customers.
words.longDefinition: Platform engineering emerged as a formalized discipline in the early 2020s in response to a problem created by the microservices era: decomposing a monolith into 50 services multiplied operational complexity by 50, imposing cognitive overhead on every product team that now needed to understand Kubernetes, Helm, Terraform, Vault, Prometheus, and CI/CD pipelines simultaneously. Platform engineering's solution is to build and maintain an Internal Developer Platform (IDP) — a curated, opinionated layer on top of the infrastructure that product engineers interact with through high-level abstractions. Key principles of platform engineering: golden paths (standardized, well-lit paths for the most common workflows — create a new service, deploy to production, rotate a secret — that work immediately without specialist knowledge); self-service (product teams provision what they need through a service catalog, portal, or CLI without filing tickets to the platform team); operator model (the platform is treated as a product with customers, feedback loops, and an SLA — not a shared service that unilaterally imposes constraints); paved roads not guardrails (making the right path easy is more effective than blocking the wrong path). Tools in the IDP ecosystem: Backstage (Spotify's open-source developer portal, adopted by hundreds of companies), Crossplane (Kubernetes-native infrastructure as code via managed resources), ArgoCD/Flux (GitOps continuous delivery), GitHub Actions/Tekton (CI pipelines), Humanitec (platform orchestrator). Platform engineering is not just infrastructure automation — it is the practice of applying product thinking and engineering excellence to the developer experience inside an organization. The DORA metrics (deployment frequency, change failure rate, mean time to recover, lead time for changes) are the platform team's KPIs.
words.connector: Think of platform engineering like the city planning department that builds roads, utilities, and zoning so that individual builders can construct houses without laying their own sewage pipes. Builders (product teams) choose what to build; the platform provides the infrastructure they build on top of — standardized, maintained, and available on demand.
words.techContext: Our platform engineering team built a service template that new microservices are provisioned from — teams get CI/CD pipeline, Kubernetes manifests, Vault secrets integration, and Datadog dashboards set up in under 30 minutes with no platform team ticket.
words.exampleSentence: After the platform team launched an internal developer portal with Backstage, the average time to onboard a new service dropped from 3 weeks to 2 days — developers no longer needed to navigate twelve separate systems to get to production.
